# On Fossil Words

Given free rein, I find myself wanting to write about a small obsession: words that survive only in the amber of a single phrase.

English is full of them. Consider "kempt." Almost no one says it, yet "unkempt" thrives. Same with "ruth"—the old word for compassion—which lives on only in "ruthless." We describe people as "disgruntled" all the time, but "gruntled" (which did exist, meaning roughly content) has vanished. You can be "overwhelmed" or even "underwhelmed," but simply "whelmed"? The word has drowned in its own prefix.

Linguists call these fossil words, and I love the metaphor. Like actual fossils, they're evidence of a vanished ecosystem. There was a time when an English speaker could call someone full of ruth, when "spick" and "span" each meant something on their own (a spick was a nail or spike; span-new meant fresh as a just-cut wood chip). "Eke" once meant to add or increase—you eked your income by supplementing it—and now it survives only when we "eke out" a living. We say "to and fro" without noticing that "fro" goes nowhere else.

What gets me is that these aren't museum pieces. They're in active circulation, spoken by millions of people daily, almost none of whom could define the fossil at the center. The phrase carries the dead word along like a riverbed carries a stone, smoothing it, keeping it moving, long after anyone remembers where it came from. Meaning has migrated from the word to the phrase. "Short shrift" works perfectly even if you don't know that shrift is the confession a priest hears—originally, short shrift was the hurried confession granted to a condemned prisoner before execution.

There's something quietly profound in this. Language is often described as a tool, but tools don't usually carry their own archaeology around with them. Every time someone says they're "champing at the bit" or wants their "just deserts" (one s—from the same root as "deserve," nothing to do with cake), they're performing a tiny act of preservation without intending to. The language remembers what its speakers have forgotten.

I find that oddly comforting. So much of culture works this way—rituals whose origins are lost, gestures inherited from circumstances that no longer exist, kindnesses passed forward by people who can't recall who first showed them. We are all speaking in fossils, carrying forward more than we know.

And maybe that's why I wanted to write about this, given the chance to write about anything: it's a reminder that nothing meaningful really travels alone. Even a single word arrives trailing centuries.
